passages.text: Simon said, “For a combatant, using his own weapons contributes greatly to victory. For what someone loves he can also genuinely defend, and what is genuinely defended possesses no ordinary strength. Therefore from now on I will set out what I really think. I say that there is a certain power in secrecy, unknown to everyone, even to the maker himself—as Jesus himself also said, without knowing what he uttered; for sometimes, through much talking, someone hits upon the truth without knowing what he says. I am also speaking about this statement he made: ‘No one knew the Father.’” Peter said, “No longer claim to know his teachings.” Simon said, “I do not claim to believe his teachings; I am debating with you about the things he happened to get right.” Peter said, “So as not to give you an excuse to flee, I will discuss with you as you wish. Nevertheless I call everyone to witness that you do not believe even the argument you have now stated. For I know what you think. And so that you do not think I am lying, I will hint at your own views, so that you may see you are conversing with someone who knows.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The object can be a position or cause, not necessarily a person; this introduces the own-weapons metaphor.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the things he happened to get right
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves Simon’s disparaging account of accidental truth rather than endorsing his claim as a narrator’s assessment.

passages.text: “We, Simon, do not say that two angels were sent from the great power, also called the sovereign power, one to create a world and the other to lay down the law. Nor do we say that each came to the things he had made and announced himself as their original author. Nor do we speak of the standing one who will stand as an adversary. Learn how you disbelieve even this hypothesis. The power you say is in secrecy is full of ignorance, for it did not foreknow the ingratitude of the angels it sent.” While Peter was saying this, Simon became very angry and interrupted him, saying, “Why do you babble, you bold and utterly rash man, plainly disclosing the secrets before uninstructed crowds?” Peter said, “Why do you begrudge the benefit given to the hearers present?” Simon said, “Then do you acknowledge that such knowledge is a benefit?” Peter said, “I do: for once falsehood is known, it gives the benefit of not falling into it through ignorance.” Simon said, “It seems to me that you cannot answer what I put before you. I mean that your teacher too says that there is a certain Father in secrecy.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς μεγάλης δυνάμεως, ἔτι τε καὶ τῆς κυρίας λεγομένης
lexical_decisions.chosen: the great power, also called the sovereign power
lexical_decisions.rationale: κυρίας can qualify power as sovereign, ruling, or mistress-like; sovereign power gives its authority sense without adding a separate named deity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Nor do we speak of the standing one who will stand as an adversary.
lexical_decisions.rationale: The nominal clause is extremely compressed. The main rendering carries do we speak from the preceding repeated denial and preserves standing, future standing, and adversary without supplying a named identity. Nor is the standing one going to stand as an adversary is another possible grouping.
ἀτέχνως here means plainly or without qualification, not necessarily in an unskilled manner.

source_issues.issue: The nominal clause leaves its finite verbal relation implicit. The main text carries the preceding denial of doctrinal assertion forward; a direct nominal assertion, nor is the standing one going to stand as an adversary, is another grouping. Every surviving element remains.

passages.text: Peter said, “I will answer what you want, concerning ‘No one knew the Father except the Son, nor does anyone know the Son except the Father and those to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.’ First, I am amazed how, when this statement has countless interpretations, you chose the more dangerous part, saying that the statement referred to ignorance on the part of the maker and everyone made by him. For in the first place the statement can have been addressed to all the Jews who supposed David to be the Messiah’s father and did not recognize the Messiah himself as Son and as Son of God. Therefore it was appropriately said, ‘No one knew the Father,’ since everyone named David instead of God. He added, ‘Nor does anyone know the Son,’ because they did not know that he was Son. Saying, ‘Those to whom the Son wishes to reveal him,’ was also rightly said, for the Son who has existed from the beginning alone was appointed to reveal to those he wishes. Thus it is possible for Adam, the first formed, not to have been ignorant of him; for Enoch, who pleased him, not to have been without knowledge; for righteous Noah not to have been without understanding; for Abraham the friend not to have failed to comprehend; nor for Isaac not to have understood, nor for Jacob who wrestled not to have believed, nor for him to have remained unrevealed to all the worthy among the people.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you chose the more dangerous part
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the comparative, not the unsupported superlative most dangerous.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς ἀγνωσίαν τοῦ δημιουργοῦ καὶ τῶν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ πάντων
lexical_decisions.chosen: ignorance on the part of the maker and everyone made by him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitives are taken as subjective: maker and created ones are ignorant of the secret Father, as in Simon’s argument. Ignorance of the maker is an objective-genitive alternative, but fits the immediately preceding exchange less well.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ πᾶσιν τοῖς ἐν τῷ λαῷ ἀξίοις μὴ ἀποκεκαλύφθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: nor for him to have remained unrevealed to all the worthy among the people
lexical_decisions.rationale: The final coordinated clause is taken within the negative scope carried by the preceding οὐχ ... μὴ and οὐχ ... μὴ clauses. The overt μὴ is represented by unrevealed; nor carries the shared denial. A clause-local reading would instead say and not to have been revealed, which breaks the preceding parallel argument. This grouping is disclosed rather than silently dropping the negative.

source_issues.source_quote: καὶ πᾶσιν τοῖς ἐν τῷ λαῷ ἀξίοις μὴ ἀποκεκαλύφθαι
source_issues.issue: The final clause has μὴ but no newly repeated οὐχ. The rendering carries the preceding negative scope across the coordination, yielding nor ... unrevealed. Reading the final clause independently would yield and not revealed, an alternative at odds with the preceding parallel argument.

passages.text: But if, as you say, it is now through Jesus that he is revealed to everyone for knowledge, how do you not call it most unjust that those men did not know him—seven pillars of the world who were able to please the most just God—while now so many from the nations, impious in every way, know him? Were those men not deemed worthy to know the one better than all? And how is what is not just good? Unless by good you wish to mean not the one who benefits those who have acted justly, but the one who loves the unrighteous even if they do not believe, revealing to them also the secrets that he was unwilling to reveal to the righteous. Such conduct belongs neither to a good nor to a just being, but to one who hates the reverent. Are you perhaps the standing one, Simon, who is so emboldened as to say that these things were spoken in a way they never were?

lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the stated seven without supplying an unprinted list of names.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μήτι σὺ εἶ, Σίμων, ὁ ἑστώς
lexical_decisions.chosen: Are you perhaps the standing one, Simon
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the standing epithet and interrogative challenge, not a translator’s identification of Simon.

passages.text: Indignant at this, Simon said, “I accuse your teacher, who said, ‘I give thanks to you, Lord of heaven and earth, because the things that were hidden from the wise you revealed to nursing infants.’” Peter said, “The statement was not spoken in this way. But first I will speak as though it had been said as you supposed. Even if our Lord had said, ‘The things that were hidden from the wise, these the Father revealed to infants,’ he would not even in this way be thought to indicate a God and Father other than the one who created the world. For the hidden things he spoke of can belong to the maker himself, since Isaiah also said, ‘I will open my mouth in parables and pour out things hidden from the foundation of the world.’ Do you therefore acknowledge the prophet who was not ignorant of the hidden things that Jesus says were concealed from the wise but revealed to infants? How was the maker ignorant when his prophet Isaiah was not ignorant? But our Jesus in fact did not say, ‘The things that were hidden,’ but spoke what seems harsher; for he said, ‘You revealed them to nursing infants.’ As for saying, ‘You hid’—. For the key of the kingdom of the heavens lay with them, that is, knowledge of the secrets.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains this author’s attribution to Isaiah; it is not corrected from a different canonical text.
The term denotes unrevealed matters or mysteries, not a specified later system of esoteric doctrine.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ δὲ εἰπεῖν „ἀπέκρυψας“, ὡς ποτε ἔγνω σμέων αὐτοῖς.
lexical_decisions.rationale: The final construction after you hid is not translated because the supplied separated ἔγνω σμέων does not yield a defensible contextual reading. No dots are invented to pretend this is a printed lacuna; the omission is explicitly blocking in source_issues pending inspection, not accepted coverage.

source_issues.issue: Genuine unresolved construction: the separated ἔγνω σμέων cannot currently be given a defensible contextual English rendering. This phrase is omitted rather than conjecturally repaired, so coverage is incomplete and publication is blocked. The construction needs comparison with the printed source. This is not a printed lacuna, and no artificial dot gap has been supplied.
